notes.extra: Sheetlike soft-tissue calcification is the visual clue. This is calcification, rather than organized cortical and trabecular bone.
The lobulated periarticular calcium deposits occur in a metabolic setting. Here metastatic refers to metabolic calcium deposition, not cancer spread.
A lobulated juxtaarticular mass at the olecranon contains amorphous calcification.
Multiple mineralized intraarticular bodies and adjacent smooth acetabular scalloping support the diagnosis.

notes.context: Young adult with a rapidly growing, painful thigh mass.
notes.extra: The peripheral zonal ossification on CT is the key discriminator. Early MRI enhancement and edema can mimic sarcoma.
Cloudlike, centrally dense mineralization represents osteoid matrix in the soft-tissue deposits.
Ring-and-arc chondroid mineralization, a costochondral origin and adjacent osseous involvement support the diagnosis.

notes.context: Young adult with a foot mass.
notes.extra: The enhancing foot mass contains internal mineralization. The vascular reconstruction maps the arterial supply; these features raise suspicion but histology establishes the tumor type.
The mass is predominantly uniform fat with only thin, architecture-preserving internal strands.
The fatty mass contains conspicuous nonfat nodules and soft-tissue strands, rather than the uniform architecture of a simple lipoma.
Thick irregular septa and nodular nonfat components make this an aggressive-appearing fatty tumor. The image does not establish an exact histologic subtype or grade.
A large predominantly fatty mass in an infant favors lipoblastoma. Age is a critical discriminator from the usual adult lipomatous tumor differential.
A rectus abdominis mass in this clinical setting supports a desmoid tumor; its attenuation is similar to muscle.

notes.context: New mass in a previously irradiated field.
notes.extra: An invasive paraspinal soft-tissue mass destroys adjacent vertebral bone and extends into the spinal canal. The prior radiation history is the essential clinical clue.
The CT angiographic reconstruction shows an extensive abnormal vascular network at the wrist.

notes.context: Mass beneath a congenital skin patch.
notes.extra: A large feeding vessel and mixed fatty and vascular components support a vascular lesion. The caption reports a capillary vascular malformation at resection.
The lesion matches subcutaneous fat on T1 and suppresses uniformly, without thick septa or a nodular nonfat component.
Entering vessels and phleboliths support a benign vascular lesion. The 2009 caption calls this a hemangioma; the images alone do not establish a modern vascular-anomaly subtype.
The cystlike T2-bright lesion has a thin enhancing rim without internal solid enhancement.
The ulnar nerve enters and exits the mass slightly eccentrically. This relationship favors schwannoma, although imaging cannot always distinguish it from neurofibroma.
The target sign has a T2-dark center and bright periphery. This caption-proven schwannoma demonstrates why the sign is not specific for neurofibroma.
The lobulated mass follows the index-finger flexor tendon sheath and is relatively low/intermediate signal on T1 and T2.

notes.context: Young adult with a groin mass.
notes.extra: Peripheral mineralization on the radiograph is more specific than the central and perilesional enhancement on MRI.
A teardrop-shaped T1-dark lesion lies in the third metatarsal interspace.
The infrascapular posterolateral chest-wall location and muscle-like signal are characteristic.
The mass is radiolucent because it contains macroscopic fat.

notes.context: Young adult with a forefoot mass.
notes.extra: Irregular soft-tissue mineralization accompanies a heterogeneous enhancing mass between the metatarsals. Histology is required to establish the tumor subtype.
The fatty portions suppress, while a distinct central nonfat component enhances.
The nodule remains T1 bright after fat suppression. Subtraction demonstrates true solid internal enhancement despite its intrinsic T1 brightness.
A plantar fascial mass has approximately muscle signal on T1 and T2, with solid enhancement.
The tendon-associated low-T2 mass blooms on the susceptibility-sensitive gradient-echo sequence because of hemosiderin.
The mass remains T1 bright with fat suppression, but subtraction shows no solid internal enhancement. A presumed hematoma that does not resolve needs reassessment.
A very T2-bright intramuscular mass shows wispy internal enhancement. Myxoid malignancies can overlap, and the illustrated diagnosis was established at biopsy.
